cues.text: From Prefect of Rome to Monk
Born around 540 to a wealthy and distinguished Roman senatorial family, Gregory received an excellent education and rose rapidly through the ranks of civil administration.
By his early thirties, he had achieved the office of Prefect of Rome — the highest civil authority in a city still nominally at the heart of what remained of the Western Roman world.
Around 575, at the height of this worldly success, Gregory renounced it entirely.
He converted his family's substantial estate on the Caelian Hill into a monastery dedicated to St.
Andrew, and gave away the remainder of his considerable wealth to found six further monasteries in Sicily and to relieve the poor.
He then entered religious life himself, seeking, as Benedict had before him, nothing more than the quiet obscurity of a monk's cell.
Fair-Haired Slaves in the Marketplace
Gregory's monastic peace did not last; the Church pulled him back into active service, first as one of the seven deacons of Rome, then as papal representative to Constantinople.
It was during these years, tradition holds, that Gregory encountered fair-haired boys being sold as slaves in the Roman marketplace.
Learning they were pagan Angles from Britain, he is said to have remarked with characteristic wit that they were not Angles but angels, so fair was their appearance.
From that moment, he resolved that this distant, unevangelized people must somehow receive the Gospel.

Gregory attempted at once to travel to Britain himself as a missionary, only to be recalled to Rome by public outcry before he had traveled more than three days from the city — a mission postponed, but never forgotten.
A Reluctant Pope
Elected pope in 590 despite his own strong preference for monastic life, he reportedly attempted to flee the city to avoid the office.
He was discovered only after a providential pillar of light revealed his hiding place.

Gregory took up the papacy at one of the most difficult moments in Rome's history: the city was suffering famine, flooding, and a devastating outbreak of plague, with civil administration in near-total collapse.

Gregory's years as a competent civil prefect proved unexpectedly essential to his papal ministry: he organized emergency grain distribution for the starving population, and negotiated directly with the threatening Lombards when imperial authority in Italy had effectively evaporated.
He also administered the vast estates of the Church with a practical, hands-on efficiency that stabilized a city otherwise abandoned by effective government.
Sending the Mission He Had Once Attempted Himself

Unable to go to Britain in person, Gregory sent the next best thing instead: around 596, a company of some forty monks, led by the prior of his own former monastery, Augustine , carried the Gospel to the pagan Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.

Gregory continued to guide the mission personally through a stream of detailed letters, offering Augustine practical, pastoral counsel on everything from adapting pagan temples for Christian worship to handling the diversity of liturgical customs the new mission would encounter.
The mission's success, converting King Æthelberht of Kent and establishing the first English archbishopric at Canterbury, earned Gregory the enduring title Apostle of the English .
It was a fulfillment, at last and by another's hand, of the missionary desire he had first felt gazing at slave children in a Roman market decades earlier.
A Prolific Pastor and Writer

Beyond his administrative and missionary labors, Gregory left the Church an extraordinary body of writing — over eight hundred surviving letters, homilies of real pastoral warmth, his Dialogues recording the lives and miracles of Italian saints including Benedict of Nursia .
He also left his Pastoral Rule , a guide to the spiritual duties of bishops that would remain required reading for Church leaders for centuries afterward.

Tradition also credits Gregory with organizing and reforming the Church's sacred chant, giving his name ever since to the tradition of Gregorian chant , whether or not he personally composed its melodies.
Legacy
Gregory died in Rome on 12 March 604, worn down by decades of relentless labor undertaken by a man who had once wanted nothing more than a quiet monastic cell.

Declared a Doctor of the Church and honored, alongside only Leo the Great, with the title "the Great," Gregory remains a model of reluctant, humble leadership pressed into extraordinary, wide-ranging service.

That same practical competence, spiritual depth, and missionary heart, when accepted rather than merely endured, can reshape the future of an entire nation that its bearer never lived to see with his own eyes.
